extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of natural philosophy / natural theology (readers of The Religious Philosopher)
extracted.subtask_description: Textual arguments that infer wisdom/providence of a Creator from anatomical, physiological, and behavioural features of birds, fishes, and other animals, illustrated with experiments and scriptural references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center of gravity and muscle placement in birds
rubrics_metrics.description: The center of gravity of birds remains in their breast below the rise of their wings, and the strong muscles that move the wings are inserted in the breast (even the muscle that raises the wings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence of 'adorable Wisdom' in creation; references Borelli (Prop. CLXXIV) and notes the surprising anatomical placement that enables effortless floating and manipulation of wings, legs, and joints. Serves as an instance of precise structural adaptation enabling flight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary strength of wing muscles relative to body weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The force of the muscles that move the wings can be many thousands of times greater than the weight of the bird that uses those wings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as astonishing but supported by Borelli (Props. CLXXXIII, CLXXXIV) and prior demonstrations of human muscle strength; presented to convince sceptics of design in muscular architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of specialized instruments in small animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Even very small birds and animals contain numerous specialized organs and instruments (for eating/digesting, generation, walking, flying) each precisely adapted to its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from complexity: the coexistence and precise adaptation of many instruments within a small body is presented as highly unlikely by chance and therefore evidence of intelligent design; rhetorical examples include sparrows, finches, canaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providential provision of food for birds
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds are kept alive seasonally and through scarcity by means that appear to provide food at the right times, demonstrating divine Providence rather than chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses scripture (Matthew vi.25-26; Luke xii.6) to support the claim; contrasts wild vs. tame animals' provision and argues that some birds receive food even when apparently deprived of means to find it, improbable by mere chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish as apparent 'miracle' of life in water
rubrics_metrics.description: The very existence of fishes that live, feed, reproduce, and perform animal functions in water, where other creatures cannot survive long, appears miraculous and requires explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used rhetorically to move skeptics from incredulity to recognition of purposeful design, highlighting the distinctness of aquatic life from aerial/terrestrial life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swim bladder as hydrostatic machine (buoyancy control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many fishes have a little bladder in the belly (swim bladder) which can be inflated or contracted by changing the air volume, allowing fishes to rise, sink, or remain suspended in water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with hydrostatic reasoning and anatomical observation (Tab. XVII Fig.5); experiments described (air-pump, hog's bladder, inverted bottle) demonstrate dilation/compression effects on buoyancy; cited Borelli (Prop. XXIX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism for regulating bladder air (communication with stomach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bladder has a small narrow tube communicating with the stomach so fishes can diminish the air by discharging through the mouth or increase it by swallowing air, enabling active control of buoyancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation used to explain fishes' ability to adapt buoyancy to seasonal and locational differences; Borelli (Prop. CXI) is cited; corroborated by experiments noting fishes expelling or swallowing air near the surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of temperature and water-column pressure on buoyancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Air volume in bladder is affected by temperature (heat dilates, cold compresses) and by depth (greater column of water increases pressure), so fishes' buoyancy changes with season and depth unless compensated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by bottle-in-receiver experiments and by reasoning about expansion/compression of entrapped air; used to argue that fishes require anatomical and behavioural means to avoid being driven unintentionally up or down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail as primary propulsive organ in fishes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fishes progress in water primarily by moving their tails back and forth, analogous to a boat's stern oar; tails are broad at the base and composed of strong membranous, flexible material moved by powerful back muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with bird wing motion; used to show form fitted to function and the wisdom of differing locomotive strategies between aquatic and aerial animals; notes extreme force in large fishes/whales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fins for balance, stopping, and steering
rubrics_metrics.description: Paired fins under the belly support fishes so their bellies remain downwards, and side fins when extended stop forward motion or when deployed asymmetrically allow turning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence: removing ventral fins causes a fish to stagger and fail to maintain natural orientation (cites Borelli Prop. CXIII); fins seen as necessary complements to tail propulsion for manoeuvrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye construction adapted to medium (water vs air)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rays of light refract differently in water than in air; fish eyes are constructed so that refraction and collection of rays occur properly in water, whereas human eyes in water produce confused vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why objects seen under water by a human appear confused; references diagram (Tab. XI Fig.2) to show refraction steps and how absence of the first refraction (at air interface) would cause blurring; used to demonstrate specific adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary fecundity of fishes as species-level design
rubrics_metrics.description: Fishes often produce an enormous number of spawn/eggs and can increase 'abundantly', a property tied to water as the producing medium and cited in scriptural text (Genesis, Psalms) as noteworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the quantity of spawn and the reproductive mechanism (external release of spawn and milt into water) are conditions pointing to purposeful design; supports with travellers' reports of abundance and scriptural language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locomotion of creeping animals via specialized musculature
rubrics_metrics.description: Creeping creatures (worms, snails) move without legs through particular arrangements of muscles (rings and longitudinal fibres) that, by alternating contraction, produce serpentine or extending motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers to Borelli and de la Hire for mechanical explanations; presented as another instance where structure (muscle arrangement) is functionally fitted, argued to be unlikely by chance and thus indicative of design.
